response.description_long:
Glowharbor sells scheduling software aimed at a specific slice of the service economy: wellness studios. The site names yoga, pilates, massage, and spa businesses as its target, positioning the product around the booking and administrative chores those businesses handle every day.

The product described is a two-sided booking system. Clients book online, pay deposits, and receive reminders, while studios manage staff calendars and class capacity from a single dashboard. That covers the core loop of a small studio: letting customers reserve time or a spot in a class, collecting some money up front to reduce no-shows, and keeping instructors and rooms from being double-booked.

Pricing is stated plainly: $29 per month per location, with a 14-day free trial. That per-location structure suggests the company expects studios that may operate more than one site, and it makes the model self-serve rather than a custom enterprise contract.

The site does not explain how the software is built, what integrations it supports, or which alternatives it replaces beyond the implicit manual or generic-tool workflow that scheduling software of this kind addresses. It also names no customers, partners, or usage figures, so there is no traction to report.

The distinctive angle, as far as the text goes, is narrowness: rather than general-purpose appointment scheduling, Glowharbor speaks directly to wellness studios and to the features those businesses care about — deposits, reminders, class capacity, and staff calendars — at a flat, published price.
